introduction.p: A series converges absolutely when the sum of its term magnitudes is finite. Absolute convergence implies convergence, regardless of the signs. This section develops the ratio and root tests for absolute convergence and Dirichlet's and Abel's tests for controlled cancellation.

exercise.title: What is the difference between absolute and conditional convergence?

statement.p: Absolute convergence means \sum |a_k| converges. Conditional convergence means the signed series converges while the absolute series diverges. In your own words, why does finite total size force ordinary convergence, and why is cancellation a weaker, more fragile reason to converge?

hint.p: If the total size is finite, the positive and negative parts are each finite, so their difference is finite. Conditional convergence keeps an infinite supply of both signs and balances them by order.

exercise.title: Why does the Ratio Test compare a series with a geometric series?

statement.p: The Ratio Test looks at \lim |a_{k+1}/a_k|. In your own words, why does a limit strictly less than 1 make the terms eventually shrink like a geometric series, and why is the test especially natural for factorials and exponentials?

hint.p: If consecutive terms are eventually no larger than a fixed fraction r<1 of the previous term, comparison with \sum r^k takes over. Factorials and exponentials change by a clean multiplicative factor from one term to the next.

exercise.title: When is the Root Test the natural test?

statement.p: The Root Test looks at \lim \sqrt[k]{|a_k|}. In your own words, why does a k-th power in the term invite a k-th root, and why is a limit strictly less than 1 again a geometric comparison?

hint.p: Taking the k-th root undoes a k-th power. If the roots settle below 1, then eventually |a_k|\le r^k for some r<1.

subsection.title: Dirichlet's and Abel's tests: controlled cancellation
subsection.p: The alternating-series test is one way to control cancellation. A more general method separates a series into a factor with bounded accumulated sums and a factor whose size changes monotonically.

paragraphs.title: Summation by parts
paragraphs.p: For integers q\ge p, put A_{p,k}=\sum_{j=p}^k a_j and A_{p,p-1}=0. Since a_k=A_{p,k}-A_{p,k-1}, expanding and shifting the finite sums gives
This is the discrete version of integration by parts. It uses only finite sums, so no convergence is assumed in the identity.

statement.p: Suppose the partial sums A_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k are bounded in absolute value, and b_n\ge0 decreases to zero. Then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_nb_n converges.

proof.p: If |A_n|\le M, with A_0=0, then |A_{p,k}|=|A_k-A_{p-1}|\le2M. Summation by parts gives
The bound tends to zero independently of q. The Cauchy criterion for series proves convergence.

subsection.p: More generally, a monotone real sequence tending to zero has one sign (or is identically zero); reversing its sign if necessary reduces it to the stated version. Taking a_n=(-1)^{n-1} recovers the alternating-series test.

example.title: Cancellation without alternating every term
example.p: follows by telescoping 2\sin(\theta/2)\sin(n\theta)=\cos((n-1/2)\theta)-\cos((n+1/2)\theta). Its magnitude is at most 1/|\sin(\theta/2)|. Thus \sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(n\theta)/n converges by Dirichlet. If \theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z, all terms are zero, so convergence holds there too. For \theta=\pi/2, the absolute-value series is 1+1/3+1/5+\cdots, which diverges by comparison with half the harmonic series. This instance is conditionally convergent.

statement.p: If \sum a_n converges and (b_n) is a bounded monotone real sequence, then \sum a_nb_n converges.

proof.p: By monotone convergence, b_n\to b for some real b. Put c_n=b_n-b. The sequence c_n is monotone and tends to zero. The partial sums of a_n are bounded because they converge. Dirichlet's test, with a sign reversal if needed, proves convergence of \sum a_nc_n. Since \sum a_nb_n=b\sum a_n+\sum a_nc_n at the level of partial sums, Abel's test follows.

example.title: A factor need not tend to zero
example.p: The alternating harmonic series converges, and b_n=2+1/n is bounded and decreasing. Abel's test therefore proves convergence of \sum(-1)^{n-1}(2+1/n)/n. Dirichlet's test with the product split in this particular way would not apply, because b_n\to2, rather than zero.

warning.title: Keep the hypotheses attached
warning.p: Bounded partial sums alone do not imply that \sum a_n converges. Also, replacing monotonicity by boundedness is invalid: \sum(-1)^n/n converges and b_n=(-1)^n is bounded, but their product is the divergent harmonic series. Abel's test here is a test for numerical series; a theorem about limits of power series at endpoints is a different result.

statement.p: Prove that \sum_{n=1}^\infty\cos(n\pi/2)/\sqrt n converges conditionally. Then use Abel's test to show that \sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^{n-1}(3-1/n)/n converges.

hint.p: The cosine partial sums are bounded; the nonzero absolute terms are 1/\sqrt{2k}, whose sum diverges. For the second series, multiply the convergent alternating harmonic series by the bounded increasing sequence 3-1/n.

exercise.title: Why does a limit of 1 give no information?

statement.p: For both the Ratio Test and the Root Test, the limit L=1 decides nothing. In your own words, why can that happen for both a divergent p-series and a convergent one, and what should you do next?

hint.p: Polynomial decay is too slow to look geometric. The same limit 1 appears for \sum 1/k and for \sum 1/k^2, so the test cannot tell them apart. Switch to comparison, the Integral Test, or the Alternating Series Test as the shape suggests.
